content.heading: 5.8 Iterative Estimates for Eigenvalues
content.paragraph: In scientific applications of linear algebra, eigenvalues are seldom known precisely. Fortunately, a close numerical approximation is usually quite satisfactory. In fact, some applications require only a rough approximation to the largest eigenvalue. The first algorithm described below can work well for this case. Also, it provides a foundation for a more powerful method that can give fast estimates for other eigenvalues as well.
content.heading: The Power Method
content.paragraph: The power method applies to an $n \times n$ matrix $A$ with a strictly dominant eigenvalue ﻿$\text{λ}_{1}$, which means that $\text{λ}_{1}$ must be larger in absolute value than all the other eigenvalues. In this case, the power method produces a scalar sequence that approaches $\text{λ}_{1}$ and a vector sequence that approaches a corresponding eigenvector. The background for the method rests on the eigenvector decomposition used at the beginning of Section 5.6.

Assume for simplicity that $A$ is diagonalizable and $\text{ℝ}^{n}$ has a basis of eigenvectors $\textbf{v}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{v}_{n}$, arranged so their corresponding eigenvalues $\text{λ}_{1},\ldots,\text{λ}_{n}$ decrease in size, with the strictly dominant eigenvalue first. That is,

From inequality (1), the fractions $\text{λ}_{2}/\text{λ}_{1},\ldots,\text{λ}_{n}/\text{λ}_{1}$ are all less than 1 in magnitude and so their powers go to zero. Hence

Thus, for large $k$, a scalar multiple of $A^{k}\textbf{x}$ determines almost the same direction as the eigenvector $c_{1}\textbf{v}_{1}$. Since positive scalar multiples do not change the direction of a vector, $A^{k}\textbf{x}$ itself points almost in the same direction as $\textbf{v}_{1}$ or $- \textbf{v}_{1}$, provided $c_{1} \neq 0$.

example.paragraph: The vectors $\textbf{x}$, $A\textbf{x},\ldots,A^{4}\textbf{x}$ are shown in Figure 1. The other vectors are growing too long to display. However, line segments are drawn showing the directions of those vectors. In fact, the directions of the vectors are what we really want to see, not the vectors themselves. The lines seem to be approaching the line representing the eigenspace spanned by $\textbf{v}_{1}$. More precisely, the angle between the line (subspace) determined by $A^{k}\textbf{x}$ and the line (eigenspace) determined by $\textbf{v}_{1}$ goes to zero as $k\rightarrow\text{∞}$.

content.paragraph: The vectors $(\text{λ}_{1})^{- k}A^{k}\textbf{x}$ in (3) are scaled to make them converge to $c_{1}\textbf{v}_{1}$, provided $c_{1} \neq 0$. We cannot scale $A^{k}\textbf{x}$ in this way because we do not know $\text{λ}_{1}$. But we can scale each $A^{k}\textbf{x}$ to make its largest entry a $1$. It turns out that the resulting sequence $\{\textbf{x}_{k}\}$ will converge to a multiple of $\textbf{v}_{1}$ whose largest entry is $1$. Figure 2 shows the scaled sequence for Example 1. The eigenvalue $\text{λ}_{1}$ can be estimated from the sequence $\{\textbf{x}_{k}\}$, too. When $\textbf{x}_{k}$ is close to an eigenvector for $\text{λ}_{1}$, the vector $A\textbf{x}_{k}$ is close to $\text{λ}_{1}\textbf{x}_{k}$, with each entry in $A\textbf{x}_{k}$ approximately $\text{λ}_{1}$ times the corresponding entry in $\textbf{x}_{k}$. Because the largest entry in $\textbf{x}_{k}$ is $1$, the largest entry in $A\textbf{x}_{k}$ is close to $\text{λ}_{1}$. (Careful proofs of these statements are omitted.)

For almost all choices of x0, the sequence {μk} approaches the dominant eigenvalue, and the sequence {xk} approaches a corresponding eigenvector.

example.heading: Example 2
example.paragraph: Apply the power method to $A = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{rr} 6 & 5 \\ 1 & 2 \end{array} \right\rbrack$ with $\textbf{x}_{0} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 0 \\ 1 \end{array} \right\rbrack$. content.paragraph: The sequence $\{\mu_{k}\}$ in Example 2 converged quickly to $\text{λ}_{1} = 7$ because the second eigenvalue of $A$ was much smaller. (In fact, $\text{λ}_{2} = 1$.) In general, the rate of convergence depends on the ratio $|\text{λ}_{2}/\text{λ}_{1}|$, because the vector $c_{2}(\text{λ}_{2}/\text{λ}_{1})^{k}\textbf{v}_{2}$ in equation (2) is the main source of error when using a scaled version of $A^{k}\textbf{x}$ as an estimate of $c_{1}\textbf{v}_{1}$. (The other fractions $\text{λ}_{j}/\text{λ}_{1}$ are likely to be smaller.) If $|\text{λ}_{2}/\text{λ}_{1}|$ is close to $1$, then $\{\mu_{k}\}$ and $\{\textbf{x}_{k}\}$ can converge very slowly, and other approximation methods may be preferred.

With the power method, there is a slight chance that the chosen initial vector $\textbf{x}$ will have no component in the $\textbf{v}_{1}$ direction (when $c_{1} = 0$). But computer rounding errors during the calculations of the $\textbf{x}_{k}$ are likely to create a vector with at least a small component in the direction of $\textbf{v}_{1}$. If that occurs, the $\textbf{x}_{k}$ will start to converge to a multiple of $\textbf{v}_{1}$.
content.heading: The Inverse Power Method
content.paragraph: This method provides an approximation for any eigenvalue, provided a good initial estimate $\alpha$ of the eigenvalue $\text{λ}$ is known. In this case, we let $B = (A - \alpha I)^{- 1}$ and apply the power method to $B$. It can be shown that if the eigenvalues of $A$ are $\text{λ}_{1},\ldots,\text{λ}_{n}$, then the eigenvalues of $B$ are
and the corresponding eigenvectors are the same as those for $A$. (See Exercises 15 and 16.)

Suppose, for example, that $\alpha$ is closer to $\text{λ}_{2}$ than to the other eigenvalues of $A$. Then $1/(\text{λ}_{2} - \alpha)$ will be a strictly dominant eigenvalue of $B$. If $\alpha$ is really close to $\text{λ}_{2}$, then $1/(\text{λ}_{2} - \alpha)$ is much larger than the other eigenvalues of $B$, and the inverse power method produces a very rapid approximation to $\text{λ}_{2}$ for almost all choices of $\textbf{x}_{0}$. The following algorithm gives the details.

note.title: The Inverse Power Method for Estimating an Eigenvalue﻿﻿ λ of A
note.heading: The Inverse Power Method for Estimating an Eigenvalue﻿﻿ λ of A

list.item: Select an initial estimate α sufficiently close to λ.
Select an initial vector x0 whose largest entry is 1.
For k=0,1,…, Solve (A−αI)yk=xk for yk. Let μk be an entry in yk with the largest absolute value. Compute νk=α+(1/μk). Compute xk+1=(1/μk)yk.
For almost all choices of x0, the sequence {νk} approaches the eigenvalue λ of A, and the sequence {xk} approaches a corresponding eigenvector.

content.paragraph: Notice that $B$, or rather $(A - \alpha I)^{- 1}$, does not appear in the algorithm. Instead of computing $(A - \alpha I)^{- 1}\textbf{x}_{k}$ to get the next vector in the sequence, it is better to solve the equation $(A - \alpha I)\textbf{y}_{k} = \textbf{x}_{k}$ for $\textbf{y}_{k}$ (and then scale $\textbf{y}_{k}$ to produce $\textbf{x}_{k + 1})$. Since this equation for $\textbf{y}_{k}$ must be solved for each $k$, an LU factorization of $A - \alpha I$ will speed up the process.

example.heading: Example 3
example.paragraph: It is not uncommon in some applications to need to know the smallest eigenvalue of a matrix $A$ and to have at hand rough estimates of the eigenvalues. Suppose $21$, $\text{3.3}$, and $\text{1.9}$ are estimates for the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ below. Find the smallest eigenvalue, accurate to six decimal places.
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: The two smallest eigenvalues seem close together, so we use the inverse power method for $A - 1.9I$. Results of a MATLAB calculation are shown in Table 3. Here $\textbf{x}_{0}$ was chosen arbitrarily, $\textbf{y}_{k} = (A - 1.9I)^{- 1}\textbf{x}_{k}$, $\mu_{k}$ is the largest entry in $\textbf{y}_{k}$, $\nu_{k} = 1.9 + 1/\mu_{k}$, and $\textbf{x}_{k + 1} = (1/\mu_{k})\textbf{y}_{k}$. As it turns out, the initial eigenvalue estimate was fairly good, and the inverse power sequence converged quickly. The smallest eigenvalue is exactly $2$.

image.alt: A table lists the k values and their corresponding x subscript k baseline, y subscript k baseline, mu subscript k baseline, and nu subscript k baseline values.

content.paragraph: If an estimate for the smallest eigenvalue of a matrix is not available, one can simply take $\alpha = 0$ in the inverse power method. This choice of $\alpha$ works reasonably well if the smallest eigenvalue is much closer to zero than to the other eigenvalues.

The two algorithms presented in this section are practical tools for many simple situations, and they provide an introduction to the problem of eigenvalue estimation. A more robust and widely used iterative method is the QR algorithm. For instance, it is the heart of the MATLAB command eig(A), which rapidly computes eigenvalues and eigenvectors of $A$. A brief description of the QR algorithm was given in the exercises for Section 5.2. Further details are presented in most modern numerical analysis texts.

Another estimate can be made for an eigenvalue when an approximate eigenvector is available. Observe that if $A\textbf{x} = \text{λ}\textbf{x}$, then $\textbf{x}^{T}A\textbf{x} = \textbf{x}^{T}(\text{λ}\textbf{x}) = \text{λ}(\textbf{x}^{T}\textbf{x})$, and the Rayleigh quotient﻿

equals $\text{λ}$. If $\textbf{x}$ is close to an eigenvector for $\text{λ}$, then this quotient is close to $\text{λ}$. When $A$ is a symmetric matrix $(A^{T} = A)$, the Rayleigh quotient $R(\textbf{x}_{k}) = (\textbf{x}_{k}^{T} A\textbf{x}_{k})/(\textbf{x}_{k}^{T}\textbf{x}_{k})$ will have roughly twice as many digits of accuracy as the scaling factor $\mu_{k}$ in the power method. Verify this increased accuracy in Exercises 11 and 12 by computing $\mu_{k}$ and $R(\textbf{x}_{k})$ for $k = 1,\ldots,4$.
Exercises 13 and 14 apply to a $3 \times 3$ matrix $A$ whose eigenvalues are estimated to be $4$, $- 4$, and $3$.

statement.paragraph: If the eigenvalues close to $4$ and $- 4$ are known to have different absolute values, will the power method work? Is it likely to be useful?
Suppose the eigenvalues close to $4$ and $- 4$ are known to have exactly the same absolute value. Describe how one might obtain a sequence that estimates the eigenvalue close to $4.$

Suppose $A\textbf{x} = \text{λ}\textbf{x}$ with $\textbf{x} \neq \textbf{0}$. Let $\alpha$ be a scalar different from the eigenvalues of $A$, and let $B = (A - \alpha I)^{- 1}$. Subtract $\alpha\textbf{x}$ from both sides of the equation $A\textbf{x} = \text{λ}\textbf{x}$, and use algebra to show that $1/(\text{λ} - \alpha)$ is an eigenvalue of $B$, with $\textbf{x}$ a corresponding eigenvector.
